before: The usual way up comes from the west, which means a long way round even though the peak stands only about three miles from Trinity. From the Trinity Trailhead, the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) climbs about 9.6 miles and 3,100 ft to Buck Creek Pass. From the pass an unmaintained high route winds around the west side of Liberty Cap and south to High Pass; contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, climb a short Class 3 step onto the ridge just south of Point 7839, and walk down into Louis Creek Basin to camp. From the basin, broad pumice, talus and low-angle snow lead up the south and southwest slopes to the crest, and loose, slabby schist with one short Class 3-4 step near a horn goes to the summit. Some parties come in over Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley instead. A direct line from King Lake on the east side exists but is brushy, involves a river ford, and is seldom used.

before.name: Snow Creek trailhead, back down the road to the driveway
before.notes:
Park at the Snow Creek trailhead on Icicle Road; the crag is a few hundred feet above the houses just downstream of the lot.

Walk back along the road about 0.1 mile to a driveway signed to the effect that hikers and climbers enter at their own risk. Follow it to a retaining wall, then take the trail rising to the right toward the crags; a sign marking the boundary onto public land appears shortly after leaving the driveway. The path continues up past smaller outcrops — about 30 minutes in total.

The lower ground is private. Start near the parking lot and traverse above the residences rather than cutting through them.
before.season: Early season — south-facing with little shade and no relief in high summer
hazards: Private land on the lower approach
A thin crux crack right off the deck on pitch one
Ledge tiers that make it easy to mistake which level you are on
before.baseFinding:
Regular Route takes the prominent dihedrals running up the middle of the biggest rock face on the crag, aiming straight at a large lone tree. Those are three independent things you can check from below: biggest face, obvious corner system, single conspicuous tree at the top of the line.

The first-pitch test is the thin crack right at the start — that is the crux of the whole route, and it is protected by bolts above the thin section. So a hard, thin opening followed by bolts confirms it; if your first pitch is easy or the corners are clean and moderate from the ground, you are on one of the upper tiers or a neighbouring route.

Everything above the first pitch is easier: clean, enjoyable dihedrals on gear from about half an inch to two inches, with small nuts and TCUs on the last pitch.

If you are at the left edge of the rock rather than in the middle of the big face, you are at Careno Corners and Bale/Kramar.

There is an obvious walk-off after pitch three, though the route carries on for a fourth.

before.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
before.notes:
Castle Rock sits right beside US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Around milepost 96.5 there is an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway; the rock is visible from the car.

Two different trails leave this one pullout and they go to different halves of the crag. For Upper Castle take the trail from the uphill, western end. It climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge, the wide bench that splits the formation in two. Ten to fifteen minutes puts you on the ledge and the first routes are five to ten minutes further.
before.season: Shoulder seasons and early or late in the day — the wall faces southwest and takes a lot of sun
hazards: Heavily polished granite that climbs harder than the grade
Full southwest sun on the upper wall
Parties above you on a crowded classic
Descent is a climbers' trail off the back of the formation down to Logger's Ledge
before.baseFinding:
Logger's Ledge is the test for every Upper Castle route: they all start from the bench, not from the ground. If you are at the foot of the rock with the highway noise still beside you, you are at Lower Castle and one full wall too low — that is the trail from the eastern end of the pullout.

On the ledge, Midway is found by the tower rather than by counting routes. It starts at Jello Tower, the pillar standing off the main wall, and the first pitch takes the corner and chimney on the tower's right side.

The adjacent feature is worth knowing so you do not confuse them: the wide crack and chimney separating the main wall from Jello Tower on the tower's west side is Damnation Crack, a much harder line at 5.9+ that starts hand-size and widens to offwidth and then chimney. If your first moves are strenuous wide climbing, you are on the wrong side of the tower.

Expect the rock to be heavily polished — this is a 1948 Beckey line and one of the most-climbed routes in the canyon, so 5.6 here does not feel like 5.6 elsewhere.

before.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
before.notes: Oversized dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the uphill, western end of the pullout; it climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
before.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Parties above you on the shared Midway terrain
before.baseFinding:
As for Midway: every Upper Castle route starts from Logger's Ledge, so if you are at the base of the rock at road level you are at Lower Castle, one wall too low.

The start is at Jello Tower — the pillar standing proud of the main wall — and the ordinary Midway line takes the corner and chimney on the tower's right side. The direct variation departs from that same feature rather than from a separate part of the ledge, so the tower is what you are looking for, not a second start.

Negative marker: the wide crack and chimney splitting the main wall from Jello Tower on its west side is Damnation Crack at 5.9+, and it climbs hands to offwidth to chimney. Strenuous wide climbing from the first moves means you are on the wrong side of the tower.

before.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge, then far right
before.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the uphill, western end of the pullout — it climbs east across the formation onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes. Then walk the ledge to its far right end.
before.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Very polished granite on the first pitch
Sandbagged for the grade because of the polish
before.baseFinding:
Saber begins from the far right end of Logger's Ledge, and the feature that names the spot is a large, low roof. The route starts on a left-angling ramp immediately to the right of that roof.

Follow the ramp up until it reaches the base of a left-facing dihedral. That dihedral is the confirmation — and the rock in it is conspicuously polished, which is itself a marker that you are on the right, heavily-travelled line.

The useful cross-check is Canary, which starts about 100 ft to the left of Saber and also on the right-hand portion of the ledge. If you have walked past a start roughly a hundred feet before this one, you passed Canary and are correctly placed.

Both routes finish on Saber Ledge, which is the reference point for the upper pitches. Note that Saber is a 1950 line rated anywhere from 5.4 to 5.6, and the polish makes it climb harder than either number suggests — do not treat it as a soft lead.

before:
AI2 ice climbing with serious commitment
Serac and objective avalanche hazard on north face
Altitude weather hazard (9,100+ ft)
Ice quality variable - sun and warmth create melting hazard
Descent complexity from exposed position

A distinct, dedicated line on the peak: an easy class 3 scramble to Emerald's twin summit block via an erosion-carved gully on the peak's west side, reached from the same North Fork Entiat trailhead (or alternately from Lake Chelan via the Emerald Park Trail).

From the Eightmile Trail, cut cross-country up through an old burn zone, then continue up and left toward the gully between the S and SE ridges. The S/SE gully is wide and offers a 'choose your own adventure' character: the center/right line is mostly class 2, while the climbers-left side holds solid class 3-4 rock. The gully tops out at roughly 8,150 ft, about 360 vertical feet below the 8,514 ft summit. This line cuts the standard 8-9 mile one-way West Ridge approach roughly in half.

Cashmere Mountain (8,514 ft), first climbed in 1900 by USGS surveyor Robert A. Farmer, is a high-prominence summit of the Wenatchee Mountains rising north of the Enchantments core above the Icicle Creek drainage. The standard West Ridge route is a long approach (roughly 17 miles round trip with about 5,300-5,500 ft of gain from the Eightmile Lake trailhead) leading to real, exposed scrambling: the upper ridge narrows into a series of tooth-like gendarmes separated by five main notches, and the final several hundred feet to the summit climb a northwest-facing gully system with sustained class 3 and a few exposed class 4 moves -- this is not a simple talus walk. Most parties camp at Lake Caroline or Little Lake Caroline (inside the Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area, which requires an overnight permit) to split the long day. The summit gives sweeping views over the core Enchantment peaks (Prusik, Dragontail, Colchuck) and the Stuart Range to the south, and Cashmere's prominence makes it a popular peak-bagging objective (58th on the Washington Bulger list).

A full-value, remote adventure alpine rock climb that is infrequently traveled and requires real route-finding rather than following an obvious line. Roughly 19 ropelengths (60m) wind up the rib and around towers: intermittent treed/sandy ledges, slabs, and short steep steps lead up an indistinct crest for about 500 vertical feet until it becomes a defined, knife-edged ridge (marked by a large open slab visible on climber's left from a distance); the rib then relaxes into low-angled, sometimes loose/sandy corners for another ~400 feet; the upper climb is steeper and more continuously exposed, featuring prominent gendarmes, a sharp ridge traverse, a left-trending ramp below a steep white headwall, and a final summit block to reach the top Beckey identifies as Crystal Lake Tower's summit.

Cold, snowy conditions from March through May give the most reliable, consolidated snow/ice; by June the couloir is warming, wetting out, and increasingly prone to rockfall and unconsolidated snow. Avoid climbing during or right after rain, heavy new snow, or a warm spell.

Lundin Peak is a jagged, three-horned summit — the westernmost horn is the true summit — on the ridge connecting Snoqualmie Mountain (6,278 ft) to Red Mountain, immediately north of Snoqualmie Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Formerly named 'Snoqualmie Little Sister,' it was renamed in 1931 to honor district forest ranger John Lundin. Short approaches from I-90 and a mix of scrambling/low-5th rock make it one of the most popular half-day alpine objectives near Seattle, but the summit block is genuinely technical: expect Class 4 and low-5th (about 5.0) climbing with real exposure on the final pitch, not a walk-up scramble.
test all talus and scree before weighting it, especially on descent — apparently solid rock can shift underfoot
turn around if the South Face is wet; the rock is considered unsafe when damp
the true (highest) summit is the westernmost of three rock horns — don't mistake a false summit for the top

Solid 5.6 climbing that rejoins the East Face route about halfway up. Instead of the standard route's loose rock, this variation deals with a moat, which parties cross by building a snow anchor with a picket and jumping the gap. 7 pitches, 1,120 ft total.

A sustained Grade III+ ice route up the broken Coleman Glacier's northwest headwall, and one of the more technically complex routes regularly climbed on Baker. From a high camp near 6,600-7,000 ft, the route crosses the broken lower Coleman Glacier to the base of the headwall around 8,500 ft, then climbs roughly 10-14 pitches of sustained 45-50 degree snow/ice with several short steeper steps (occasionally 60-80 degrees) and a crux bergschrund passage near 10,000 ft before easing onto the summit plateau. Most parties start well before dawn and take 8-12 hours camp-to-summit.

Grade III, 5.6 on the ridge. From Boston Basin high camp, traverse glacier to Sharkfin Col via 10 feet of 5.7 rock and 200 feet of Class 3 gully. North ridge route at ~7,700 ft to summit. Moderate to good granite, high exposure with wonderful ridge position. Glaciers: Quien Sabe Glacier, Boston Glacier.

before.notes: Approximately 50 feet to the summit horn. Fixed pitons and an old fixed cam are present but should not be relied upon as the sole anchor. The crux is a brief section, graded 5.5 to 5.7, on reasonably solid rock. Belayed ascent is standard; an inverted V rappel anchor is established at the top by modern parties. Excellent protection available from both natural features and fixed gear. The moves are sustained and exposed.

before: Grade III alpine rock, 5.11 crux. Four pitches on Liberty Bell West Face. Pitch 1 (5.8): Slab moves left into corner with short bulge. Pitch 2 (5.11 crux): Wide hand crack, physical, excellent gear. Pitch 3 (5.10): Left-angling hand crack with roof/bulge exit. Pitch 4 (5.7): Navigate tunnel or harder left slab variation, then simul/scramble on exposed sunny arete to summit. Approach via Beckey Route approach, staying left at fork in gully. Excellent hand crack climbing with minimal traffic. Hazards: loose rock from freeze-thaw cycles, afternoon thunderstorms, exposure on final arete.

Liberty Crack is the most celebrated route on Liberty Bell and #24 in Roper & Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America, splitting the steep, 1,200-foot east face with a soaring line of cracks. The signature roof on Pitch 2, the 'Lithuanian Lip,' is named for Alex Bertulis' Lithuanian heritage — he made an unsuccessful attempt on the roof in 1964 with Steve Marts before Marts, Don McPherson, and Fred Stanley completed the route the following year. Most parties fix and aid the crux Pitches 2-3 (or free them at 5.11-5.13-) and climb the remaining pitches free before topping out on the Beckey Route's final slab.

Clean Break rises 1,500 feet above the valley floor on the steep east buttress of Juno Tower, taking its name from the immaculate splitter-crack at pitch 1. With several of its 15 pitches at 5.10, this sustained granite route is regarded as one of the finest long multi-pitch climbs at this grade in Washington.

Descend via the Cascadian Couloir, the standard walk-off for the entire Stuart massif — this is a scramble descent, not a rappel route, under normal (dry to firm-snow) conditions. From the summit, reverse the short 3rd/2nd-class scramble west along the summit ridge to the false summit (~9,200 ft), then drop into the broken rock and scree above the top of the couloir. Stay climber's-right through sparse trees and rock bands near the top to find the true couloir entrance rather than dropping into parallel gullies to the left, which cliff out. From there it's a sustained, direct descent of loose scree/talus (snow early season) losing about 4,000 ft to the floor of the Ingalls Creek valley — many parties glissade or boot-ski the upper snowfield when it's in, which is markedly faster and easier on the knees than the bare-scree version later in summer. Watch for sun cups and inconsistent snow texture on the upper couloir, and expect significant rockfall exposure funneled by the gully, especially with other parties above or below. At the bottom, pick up a climber's path through meadows to the Ingalls Creek Trail near the Longs Pass turnoff, then reverse the approach (back over Longs Pass) to the Esmeralda Trailhead. No rappels are required on this descent in normal conditions; a fixed/natural rock anchor has been reported near the false summit that some parties use to rappel the initial short, steep, icy step off the summit ridge in early-season or verglassed conditions, but this is a discretionary variation, not a standard part of the descent, and the anchor is not maintained or guaranteed. Total summit-to-trailhead time is commonly 3–5 hours for a fit party in good conditions.

From the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead, follow Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows to the Surprise Lake loop and take its right fork to the trail's high point. Leave the trail there, climb west into a basin, cross it left of some large mounds and drop briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier. Climb the glacier (now largely a series of persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier) near the center of the cirque, right of the rock band that splits the upper and lower sections, then right of the snow dome to gain the ridge. A rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to a small saddle just east of the true summit, and a short, loose class 3 scramble finishes it. Popular and the most straightforward line up the peak, though it is a long outing (~20 miles round trip) with real elevation gain.

Drive to the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead (Trail #1120, elev. ~4,044 ft): from Naches, WA take US-12 W about 22 miles, turn onto Forest Road 1200 (Tieton Reservoir Road) for 4.5 miles, then onto Forest Road 1000 (South Fork Tieton Road) for 12.6 miles to the trailhead at road's end (last ~7 miles gravel, generally in good condition). Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows (crossing Conrad Creek) into the Goat Rocks Wilderness, continuing to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin; cross it left of some large mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

before.notes: Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows to the Surprise Lake loop, then the loop's right fork to the trail's high point.
Off-trail west into a basin, crossing it left of some large mounds, then a short descent to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

Up the Meade near the center of the cirque, right of the rock band between the upper and lower glacier, then right of the snow dome to the ridge. Crampons recommended; moats and crevasses can open late in the season.
A rough goat and boot path on the southwest side to a small saddle, then a short, loose scramble west to the true summit; exposed in places, and the rock is unstable.

before.name: Conrad Meadows and the Surprise Lake loop to the Meade Glacier
before.notes:
Drive to the Conrad Meadows and South Fork Tieton trailhead at road's end, about 4,044 ft, reached by the Tieton Reservoir road and then the South Fork Tieton road off the highway west of Naches. The last several miles are gravel.

Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows, crossing Conrad Creek, into the Goat Rocks Wilderness and on to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin. Cross it left of some large mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

This is a long day: roughly 20 miles round trip with real gain, and limited water late in a dry season.
hazards: A steep snowfield below the summit requiring solid self-arrest
Loose rock on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk between parties climbing close together
A receding glacier that can still hide crevasses and moats
A long, remote round trip of roughly 20 miles with limited water in a dry year
Basin navigation that depends on visibility once off the trail
before.baseFinding:
Leaving the trail in the right place and finding the foot of the Meade is the whole route-finding problem, and everything before it is trail.

Take the right fork of the Surprise Lake loop and stay on it to its high point. From there climb west into a basin, cross it keeping left of the large mounds, and drop a short way to the foot of the glacier. If you are climbing onto a long ridge crest before you have reached any snow, you are on the ridge line to the south, not this route.

On the glacier, one rock band organises everything. It splits the lower glacier from the upper; go up near the center of the cirque and pass it on its right. Above it, stay right of the snow dome and the ridge comes easily.

The base of the scramble is a small saddle, and the summit is just west of it. From the ridge a rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to that saddle; the true summit is immediately to its west, a short, loose class 3 scramble. If the ground keeps rising well beyond a gap, you are at the wrong gap.

The negative that separates this from its sibling on the same peak: this line reaches the Meade from below, out of the basin. The other route from this trailhead crosses the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle east of the summit and drops onto the Meade from above. If you are on the Conrad Glacier, you are on that one instead.

Self-arrest is part of the base finding here, not an afterthought: the snowfield below the summit is steep enough that the route assumes you can hold a slip on it. Arriving without an axe is a reason to turn round at the foot of the glacier.

before: Approach from Summerland alpine meadow via the Fryingpan Glacier, aiming southwest toward Whitman Crest notch at 9,000 feet. Cross the Whitman Glacier and ascend to the summit block, where a short but serious Class 4 scramble (30-40 feet) on loose andesite reaches the true summit. The route is graded as a moderate alpine climb, feasible for competent glacier climbers but not for beginners.
A sustained, direct line dropping off Liberty Cap on Rainier's northwest side, from roughly 13,400' to 9,900'; best documented as a ski-mountaineering descent rather than an ascent route.

A prominent snow/ice couloir ('finger') splitting the cliffs between the Nisqually and Wilson Glaciers, giving one of the more direct lines up Rainier's south side. From Paradise the route crosses the Nisqually Glacier to high camps on Wapowety Cleaver at the edge of the Wilson Glacier, then crosses the Wilson Glacier and climbs a narrowing gully at 35-45° that leads onto the upper Nisqually Glacier; the Finger itself pinches to a few hundred feet wide at roughly 40-50°. Above the Finger the route continues up the upper Nisqually Glacier to about 13,000 ft, where it joins the upper Kautz Glacier line and the angle eases toward the summit.
Descend Emmons-Winthrop to White River

A notorious ~3,600-foot north face — the headwall of the Carbon Glacier's cirque — capped by a 200-300 ft band of hanging ice (seracs) that has historically deterred most attempts and is the wall's defining objective hazard. Named for geological engineer Bailey Willis, who helped build the first trail to the Carbon Glacier in 1881. The wall's West Rib was first climbed in June 1961 by Charles ('Charlie') Bell, though credit for the first ascent was disputed for years; Jim Wickwire (who climbed the East Rib in 1963 and made the first winter ascent in 1970) later corroborated Bell's claim by comparing notes and photographs directly with Bell.
